title: Core ideas in economics
description: The handful of ideas economists use to explain prices, trade, incentives and growth.

ideas.title: Scarcity and opportunity cost
ideas.summary: Because resources are limited, every choice has a cost: the best alternative you gave up.

items.q: In economics, what is opportunity cost?
items.a: The value of the best alternative you give up when you make a choice

items.q: You skip a work shift that pays $80 to go to a free concert. In money terms, what is the concert's opportunity cost?
items.a: $80, the pay you gave up

items.q: What does it mean to "think at the margin" in economics?
items.a: To weigh the extra benefit of one more unit against its extra cost

items.q: What is the law of diminishing marginal utility?
items.a: Each additional unit of a good gives less extra satisfaction than the one before

items.q: In economics, what is a sunk cost, and how should it affect a decision?
items.a: A cost already paid that cannot be recovered; it should be ignored when deciding what to do next

ideas.title: Supply, demand and price
ideas.summary: Prices move to balance what buyers want with what sellers offer, and they carry information to both.

items.q: What does the law of demand say?
items.a: Other things equal, when the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls

items.q: In a market, what is the equilibrium price?
items.a: The price at which the quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded

items.q: What results when a price ceiling, such as rent control, is set below the equilibrium price?
items.a: A shortage: the quantity demanded exceeds the quantity supplied

items.q: A frost destroys much of the orange crop. What happens to the price of oranges, and why?
items.a: It rises, because supply has fallen while demand is unchanged

items.q: Which Scottish economist described the "invisible hand" in "The Wealth of Nations" (1776)?
items.a: Adam Smith

ideas.title: Trade and specialization
ideas.summary: People and countries gain by specializing in what they give up least to produce, and trading for the rest.

items.q: In economics, what is comparative advantage?
items.a: The ability to produce something at a lower opportunity cost than others can

items.q: Which British economist set out the theory of comparative advantage in 1817?
items.a: David Ricardo

items.q: What is the difference between absolute advantage and comparative advantage?
items.a: Absolute: producing more with the same resources; comparative: producing at a lower opportunity cost

items.q: In Adam Smith's example of the pin factory, what makes the workers so much more productive?
items.a: The division of labor: each worker specializes in one step

ideas.title: When markets fail
ideas.summary: Markets misfire when costs fall on bystanders, when a resource is shared by all, or when someone else bears the risk.

items.q: In economics, what is an externality?
items.a: A cost or benefit of an activity that falls on people who are not party to it

items.q: A factory's smoke dirties its neighbors' laundry, and the factory pays nothing for it. What do economists call this cost?
items.a: A negative externality

items.q: What is the tragedy of the commons?
items.a: A shared resource is overused because each user takes the full benefit while everyone shares the cost

items.q: Which two properties define a public good?
items.a: Non-excludable and non-rival: no one can be shut out, and one person's use leaves no less for others

items.q: In economics, what is moral hazard?
items.a: Taking more risk because someone else bears the cost, as people may when insured

ideas.title: Money, growth and the whole economy
ideas.summary: Macroeconomics tracks total output and the price level, and the tools governments and central banks use to steady them.

items.q: What does gross domestic product (GDP) measure?
items.a: The market value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a given period

items.q: In economics, what is inflation?
items.a: A sustained rise in the general level of prices

items.q: What is the difference between fiscal policy and monetary policy?
items.a: Fiscal: government taxing and spending; monetary: the central bank's control of money and interest rates

items.q: In economics, what is the difference between nominal and real values?
items.a: Real values are adjusted for inflation; nominal values are not

items.q: By the rule of 72, roughly how long does an amount growing at 6% a year take to double?
items.a: About 12 years (72 divided by 6)
